title: A quarter of the price
hook: Most homes use soap bars because powder costs too much. You can make powder cheaper. How low can you price it?
role: You make and sell a washing powder, 1969 to the 1990s

future.label: Reach
future.hint: How many homes buy your powder

intro.text: Gujarat, 1969. You are a 24-year-old chemist in a government lab. After work, at home, you make a yellow washing powder that cleans well. But most families still use soap bars because powder costs too much. With a job, a bicycle and a small room, can you get your powder into ordinary homes?

d1.title: Set the price
d1.setup: You buy simple materials nearby and mix the powder yourself, so your costs are low. Now you need to set a price for each kilo. The big brand, Surf, costs about ₹13 a kilo and sells to richer homes in the cities. Everyone else uses soap bars because they cannot spend much on washing.
d1.question: What price do you put on a kilo?
d1.advisor: A low price may bring more buyers, but you earn less on each kilo. A high price gives you more per kilo, but fewer homes may be able to pay.

options.label: Price it near Surf, at about ₹12 a kilo, so it seems like a quality powder.
options.outcome: Shopkeepers ask why they should stock an unknown powder at Surf's price. The few homes that can pay ₹12 stay with the brand they know. You sell only a few packets a week, while most of your powder stays in your room.
options.why: Remember: your low cost was your strength, but the high price did not use it. You fought Surf where it was strongest, and only richer homes could pay.
options.better: Price it near what soap-bar homes already spend, about a quarter of Surf, and earn by selling much more.
options.takeaway: In 1969 you priced like the big brand. A low cost only helps you if your price uses it.

options.label: Price it at about ₹9 a kilo, well under Surf, and keep a good profit on each kilo.
options.outcome: A few Surf buyers switch to save money, and you earn well on each packet. But ₹9 is still too much for soap-bar homes, so your sales grow slowly.
options.why: Remember: a good profit on each kilo means little if few people buy. The bigger market was the soap-bar homes, not Surf's buyers.
options.better: Go down to about a quarter of Surf's price, so soap-bar homes can switch, and earn from selling much more.
options.takeaway: In 1969 you chose a safe middle price. A good profit on a few sales still adds up to little.

options.label: Price it at ₹3.50 a kilo, about a quarter of Surf, close to what soap-bar homes spend.
options.outcome: At ₹3.50 a kilo, your powder costs about the same as a soap bar and washes far better. After work, you cycle from door to door and sell 15 to 20 packets a day with a money-back promise. In Ahmedabad, word starts to spread.
options.why: Remember: when each kilo leaves you very little, you need low costs and many buyers. Your costs were tiny, so even this low price left a little on each kilo. Now millions of soap-bar homes could afford it.
options.takeaway: In 1969 you priced for many buyers, not a few. A thin margin works when costs are low and sales are high.

d2.title: Home or factory?

setup.text: Orders grow one street at a time. You still mix and pack every kilo at home in a ten-foot by ten-foot room, then go to your government job each day. A small factory could make far more, but its rent and wages must be paid every month, whether sales come or not.

Sales are slow, but you believe they can grow. You still mix and pack every kilo at home in a ten-foot by ten-foot room, then go to your government job each day. A small factory could make far more, but its rent and wages must be paid every month, whether sales come or not.

d2.question: Orders are growing slowly. How do you make the powder now?
d2.advisor: Your room limits how much you can make, but sales are still small. A factory gives you more space, but its rent comes every month whether you sell ten packets or ten thousand.

options.label: Keep your job. Make it at home after work, and grow only as orders grow.
options.outcome: For about three years, you work two jobs. Your salary pays the bills at home, while every packet you sell adds to the business. Around 1972, with orders growing, you leave the government job and work on your powder full time.
options.why: Remember: break-even is the sales needed to pay your fixed costs. With almost no rent or wages, even a few packets a day could cover your costs. Your costs grew only when your buyers did.
options.takeaway: In 1969 you kept your costs tiny until the buyers came. Low fixed costs mean you break even sooner.

options.label: Quit your job and rent a small factory, so you can make far more.
options.outcome: The factory can make ten times what your room could, but rent, wages and the power bill come every month while sales are still growing. Within months, your savings are nearly gone, and you have no salary to fall back on.
options.why: Remember: break-even is the sales needed to pay your fixed costs. Rent and wages are fixed costs. They arrived before enough buyers did, so each month ended in a loss.
options.better: Keep costs tiny until sales prove the demand. Move to a factory when your orders are more than your room can handle.
options.takeaway: In 1969 you built a factory before the buyers came. Early fixed costs raise the sales you need just to break even.

options.label: Pay a local maker to mix and pack it. No rent, but he charges for every kilo.
options.outcome: You pay no rent, and you can sell far more than your room could make. But the maker charges for every kilo, and at your low price, almost nothing is left. As sales grow, he earns more while you earn very little.
options.why: Remember: fixed costs stay the same, but variable costs rise with every sale. The maker's charge was added to every kilo. With such a thin margin, that cost took most of what you earned.
options.better: While sales are small, make it yourself at almost no cost, so each kilo still leaves a little. Bring in a factory once orders outgrow your room.
options.takeaway: In 1969 you paid someone for every kilo. With a thin margin, a cost on every sale takes away most of your profit.

text.text: The business is now your full-time work. Instead of using many traders, your packets go from one distributor straight to the shops. You focus on small towns, not the rich areas where Surf is strong. Plain plastic pouches keep costs low, and from 1975 a catchy radio song sings your powder's name.

You keep going, and slowly the factory gets enough orders to stay busy. Distributors take your packets to shops in small towns where Surf is weak, and from 1975 a catchy radio song sings your powder's name. But the early losses still hurt the business.

The maker keeps your packets coming. Distributors take them to shops in small towns where Surf is weak, and from 1975 a catchy radio song sings your powder's name. Sales grow, but each kilo still leaves you very little.

d3.title: The shops won't pay
d3.setup: Thanks to your ads, buyers now ask for your powder by name, and it sits in shops across many towns. But shopkeepers want credit, or udhaar. They take your stock, sell it, and then pay late, or not at all. Cash coming in drops, while you still need cash to buy raw materials.
d3.question: What do you do about the money the shops owe you?
d3.advisor: The shops bring us buyers, so losing them would hurt. But every rupee they owe us is money we cannot use today.

options.label: Keep giving credit. It's how shops work, and you can't afford to lose them now.
options.outcome: The shops stay happy and keep ordering, but what they owe you grows every month. Your books show a profit, yet you do not have enough cash for raw materials. Soon, you cannot make enough powder to fill orders.
options.why: Remember: credit, or udhaar, is a loan you give. A business can show a profit in its books while it has no cash. You were lending to every shop with no limit and no pay date.
options.better: Treat credit like a loan: give each shop a limit and a pay date, or ask for cash.
options.takeaway: When shops paid late, you kept giving credit. Udhaar is a loan you give, so manage it like one.

options.label: Take your unsold packets back from the shops. Supply again only to shops that pay cash.
options.outcome: You pull more than nine in ten packets out of the market while your ads keep playing. For about a month, buyers ask for your powder but cannot find it. Then the shopkeepers come to you, and this time they pay cash first.
options.why: Remember: credit, or udhaar, is a loan you give, so manage it like one. Your ads had already made buyers want your powder. When they kept asking for it, you could ask shops to pay cash first.
options.takeaway: When shops paid late, you took back your stock and asked for cash. When buyers want your product, you can set the terms.

options.label: Borrow from a bank to cover the cash gap. Keep supplying shops while you wait for them to pay.
options.outcome: The loan keeps raw materials coming, but the shops still pay late. Now you also pay the bank interest every month, so you are lending to the shops with money you borrowed.
options.why: Remember: a business can show a profit in its books while it has no cash. The loan helped for a while, but it did not fix the late payments. You paid the bank interest while the shops paid you nothing extra.
options.better: Fix the cause first. Make the shops pay cash, or by a fixed date, before you borrow.
options.takeaway: When shops paid late, you borrowed to cover their udhaar. A loan can help for a while, but the shops still owe you.

text.text: In 1982 your first TV ad goes on air, and the jingle becomes famous. In 1985 your powder passes Surf as India's best-selling detergent, and by 1988 more than half the market is yours. Surf's maker, Hindustan Lever, takes years to answer. In the end, it brings out a cheap powder of its own.

In 1982 your first TV ad goes on air, and the jingle becomes famous. With cash coming in at last, your powder catches up with Surf in many towns. Then Surf's maker, Hindustan Lever, brings out a cheap powder of its own.

In 1982 your first TV ad goes on air, and people like the jingle. But cash stays tight, so you cannot always fill the orders that the ads bring in. Surf's maker, Hindustan Lever, sees its chance and brings out a cheap powder of its own.

d4.title: Buy or build?

setup.text: It is the mid-1990s. Your powder leads the market, but Hindustan Lever spends many times more on ads than you do. You still buy your main chemicals from other companies, so every kilo includes their price and their profit.

It is the mid-1990s. Your powder is a known name, but Hindustan Lever spends many times more on ads than you do. You still buy your main chemicals from other companies, so every kilo includes their price and their profit.

d4.question: How do you keep your price the lowest?
d4.advisor: Building our own chemical plants would cost more than a thousand crore rupees, and we would pay before the plants make anything. Buying from others costs less now, but they decide the prices we pay.

options.label: Build your own chemical plants. It costs a huge sum now and will take years to pay off.
options.outcome: You build a plant near Vadodara to make LAB, the main cleaning chemical in your powder, and plan a giant plant for soda ash, another key chemical, near Bhavnagar. Once both are running, you expect each kilo of powder to cost another 25% less to make.
options.why: Remember: a plant is a fixed cost. You pay for it once, however much you sell. Small fixed costs were right when your sales were unproven. Now you sell crores of packets, so the plant makes every kilo cheaper.
options.takeaway: In the 1990s you spent big once to make every kilo cheaper. At high volume, a fixed cost can cut the cost of each sale.

options.label: Keep buying chemicals, and spend the money on far more ads instead.
options.outcome: Your ads get bigger and louder, but Hindustan Lever can always spend more. Your chemical bill still grows with every kilo you sell, and your price lead becomes smaller. Shoppers begin to see two similar powders at similar prices.
options.why: Remember: your strength was low cost. Ads did nothing to lower the cost of each kilo, and you spent your money competing with a rival that could spend more.
options.better: Spend once on your own plants so every kilo you sell stays cheaper.
options.takeaway: In the 1990s you fought a rich rival with ads. Your edge was low cost, so protect that first.

options.label: Sign long deals with chemical makers that lock their price for years.
options.outcome: The deals keep your costs steady for a few years, and you spend nothing on plants. But when the deals end, the sellers raise their prices. Every kilo you sell still includes their profit.
options.why: Remember: a locked price is not a lower price. The chemicals still cost you on every kilo, and the sellers still kept their profit.
options.better: With sales this big, make the chemicals yourself. One large cost now can make every kilo cheaper.
options.takeaway: In the 1990s you locked in a price instead of making the chemicals yourself. A fixed price is not the same as a lower cost.

text.text: From a small room at home, you built India's best-selling washing powder. It passed Surf in 1985, and in the 1990s you began making your own chemicals to keep costs low. You showed that millions of soap-bar homes would buy powder if the price was right.
You made a few different choices, but your low costs kept the business strong. Now your powder is a name that almost every home in India knows.

survivor.title: A good regional brand
survivor.text: Your powder sells well in many towns, and the business pays its way. But you never fully used your low cost, and Surf's maker keeps most of India's homes.

collapse.title: Off the shelves
collapse.text: Your costs grow faster than your sales, and cash keeps running short. Bigger brands with cheap powders take your place on the shelves. Slowly, your packets disappear from the shops.

fired.title: Back to a day job
fired.text: After three costly decisions, the money runs out. Your distributors no longer trust you to deliver, and the bank won't lend again. You close the business and go back to working for someone else.

realHistory: In 1969 a young government chemist in Gujarat made a cheap yellow washing powder at home and sold it for about ₹3.50 a kilo, when Surf cost about ₹13. He sold it door to door by bicycle after work, kept his costs very low, and went full time around 1972. When shops paid late, he pulled his stock back while his ads kept running, and the shops agreed to pay cash. The radio jingle began in 1975 and the first TV ad in 1982. Nirma passed Surf in 1985 and had about 60% of the detergent market by 1988. Hindustan Lever answered late with its own cheap powder, Wheel. In the 1990s Nirma went public and built its own raw material plants to cut costs further.
